title: Hierarchical connectivity sets the upper critical dimension of neural avalanches
abstract: Neural avalanches with size exponent $3/2$ are usually explained by mean-field critical branching, which for short-range coupling requires dimension $N\ge4$. We show that hierarchical connectivity removes this constraint. In a $p$-adic version of the Buice--Cowan field theory, a coupling that decays by $p^{-(N+σ)}$ per hierarchical level selects the Taibleson--Vladimirov operator, and the critical theory is ultrametric directed percolation with upper critical dimension $N_c=2σ$. Exact simulations on a tree give $τ_S=3/2$ for $σ\le N/2$, decreasing continuously for $σ>N/2$.
summary: This paper investigates neural avalanches on networks with hierarchical connectivity modeled using $p$-adic mathematics. It shows that this structure bypasses dimensional constraints typically found in mean-field theories, establishing a new upper critical dimension $N_c=2\sigma$. The work provides a theoretical framework for understanding how connectivity decay dictates the critical behavior of complex, non-equilibrium physical systems.
main_problem: The paper addresses determining the upper critical dimension for neural avalanches when the underlying connectivity is hierarchical, contrasting with standard mean-field predictions.
main_result: Hierarchical connectivity removes the constraint that $N \ge 4$ required for mean-field behavior, establishing the upper critical dimension as $N_c = 2\sigma$.
method: The analysis uses a $p$-adic formulation of the Buice--Cowan field theory, deriving the effective theory via the Taibleson–Vladimirov operator.
model_or_system: The model describes cortical activity propagating in neuronal avalanches, formulated on the $p$-adic numbers ($\mathbb{Q}_p$) which naturally impose a tree-like, ultrametric structure.

important_parameters: The coupling decay rate $\sigma$, the dimension $N$, and the parameter $p$ defining the $p$-adic structure.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the $p$-adic structure ($\mathbb{Q}_p$) and assumes the validity of the Ginzburg criterion to assess mean-field breakdown.

paper_structure: The paper progresses by setting up the generalized Doi–Peliti action on $\mathbb{Q}_p$, deriving the effective theory using the Taibleson–Vladimirov operator, establishing the critical dimension $N_c=2\sigma$, and finally comparing mean-field predictions against simulation results on the tree structure.
why_interesting: While focused on neural dynamics, the use of $p$-adic analysis and the study of critical phenomena in structured, non-Euclidean lattices provides mathematical tools relevant to analyzing complex, disordered quantum systems or quantum networks with inherent hierarchical structure.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Neurons organized in a tree-like structure (p = 2, depth 4: levels 0, . . . , 4). The p-adic distance between two neurons is determined by the level of their last common an- cestor. With a kernel w(∥x∥p) ∝∥x∥−N−σ p , the exponent σ measures how fast coupling decays with hierarchical distance.

FIG. 2. Connection matrices wij of two networks of 64 neurons with σ = 1 (logarithmic color scale; diagonal excluded; total coupling per neuron normalized to 1). (a) Hierarchical network, p = 2, N = 1, l = 6, wij ∝|i −j|−(1+σ) 2 . Neurons are ordered along the boundary of the tree; the nested blocks are the modules of levels 5, 4, . . . , 1, and w is constant on each block. (b) Euclidean ring with wij ∝|i −j|−(1+σ).

FIG. 3. Avalanches at the critical point. (a) Probability that an avalanche has size at least S, for the hierarchical network (p = 2, N = 1, l = 40) with five values of σ, and for a Euclidean chain with nearest-neighbor coupling. Dotted lines: the mean-field law S−1/2 (τS = 3/2) and the DP law S−0.108 in one dimension. (b) τS against σ. Filled circles: maximum-likelihood fit of the size distribution (10 ≤S ≤2000). Open squares: τS = 1 + δ/(1 + ϑ + δ) from the measured survival and growth exponents. The vertical line marks σ = N/2, where N = Nc.
